title: YOLO-RoadSurvey: Real-Time Traffic Monitoring and Pavement Damage Detection for Bandung Roadways

authors.name: Rizky Putra
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: City authorities in Bandung, Indonesia, need automated tools to quantify traffic flow and detect pavement damage for maintenance planning and safety. Traditional manual surveys and classical image methods require extensive human hours and fall below acceptable accuracy when lighting or occlusion vary. Recent single-stage detectors report high detection rates but either run only on desktop GPUs or drop accuracy under small-object or low-light conditions. This work presents YOLO-RoadSurvey, a real-time edge system combining a tailored YOLOv5-lite model, geometry-aware postprocessing, and a lightweight road-crack classifier to perform simultaneous vehicle counting and pavement damage localization on Jetson Nano hardware. On a mixed urban dataset collected across 12 Bandung road segments (7,500 labeled images), the combined pipeline achieves 95.4% detection accuracy for vehicle presence, mean average precision (mAP@0.5) of 0.912 for damage localization, end-to-end latency of 12.3 ms per frame (measured at 320x320 input), and F1-score of 0.947 for crack classification. Power draw averaged 3.2 W under inference load. These numbers meet municipal targets for automated survey (latency <= 20 ms, accuracy >= 90%). The system can be deployed on existing traffic poles and can reduce inspection labor by an estimated 76% while enabling monthly trend reports for maintenance scheduling.

content.text: Bandung's municipal transport office schedules road inspections across an aging urban network of asphalt and concrete sections; manual surveys are labor-intensive and slow to scale. Inspections in 2023 covered 1,200 km of carriageway but required teams on-site for visual logging and manual counting (Dinas Bina Marga Kota Bandung reports). Automated camera-based approaches promise faster coverage and repeatable metrics. Yet city planners still lack a field-proven, low-cost system that simultaneously counts traffic and flags pavement distress under varied sunlight, rain, and occlusion conditions.

Recent work has advanced single-shot object detectors and crack classifiers. Redmon et al. introduced YOLOv3 on GPU with 57.9% mAP on COCO at 45 ms inference on a Titan X [4], but the model requires desktop-class GPUs and suffers on small objects. Bochkovskiy et al. reported YOLOv4 with 43.5% COCO mAP at 62 fps on RTX2080, yet the official model grows to 244 MB making edge use difficult [3]. Liu et al. proposed SSD on mobile CPUs reaching 72.1% mAP on PASCAL VOC at 30 ms on a CPU but missed thin cracks and small potholes [5]. The RDD2018 benchmark achieves 84.7% damage detection with classical CNNs trained on high-resolution road images, but accuracy dropped to 68.2% when images were captured from poles at 6 m height (simulating city installations) [6]. Finally, recent lightweight approaches such as MobileNetV2-based detectors hit 82–88% accuracy on vehicle counting on test roads but report latency above 25 ms on Jetson Nano, exceeding municipal targets [8], [11].

The concrete gap is clear: accuracy often falls below 80% for pavement distress when images are acquired from 4–8 m pole-mounted cameras with variable lighting, and latency frequently exceeds 20 ms on embedded hardware required for distributed deployment. Moreover, many prior pipelines treat traffic counting and pavement damage as separate tasks, requiring duplicated hardware or sequential processing that increases power and data costs. What remains unsolved is a single, low-power pipeline that maintains at least 90% vehicle detection accuracy, localizes damage with mAP >= 0.85 from pole heights, and runs below 20 ms per frame on an off-the-shelf embedded board.

We propose YOLO-RoadSurvey, a practical system integrating a YOLOv5-lite backbone, geometry-aware non-maximum suppression (NMS), and a small convolutional classifier for crack versus pothole discrimination. The main contributions are listed below: 
• A tailored YOLOv5-lite network trained on a mixed Bandung dataset (7,500 images) achieving 95.4% vehicle detection accuracy and 0.912 mAP@0.5 for damage localization when run at 320×320 input on Jetson Nano (measured, reproducible numbers). 
• A geometry-aware postprocessing stage that raises small-object recall by 6.2 percentage points compared to vanilla NMS and reduces false positives on wet road surfaces. 
• A field-ready hardware and software stack demonstrated on 12 road segments in Bandung, with measured latency of 12.3 ms per frame and average power draw of 3.2 W, enabling live monthly traffic and damage reports for municipal planners.

Section II reviews related work in object detection for traffic, crack/pothole detection, and edge deployment strategies. Section III describes system design: architecture, hardware selection, algorithmic details, and communication. Section IV presents the experimental protocol, results, comparisons, and endurance tests. Section V discusses limitations and outlines next steps for scaling across West Java.

This section reviews three literature threads that inform YOLO-RoadSurvey: single-stage detectors for traffic and small-object detection; automated pavement distress detection; and edge deployment strategies for embedded inference. Each thread contains practical results and constraints that we link directly to our design choices (dataset augmentation, model slimming, and geometry-aware postprocessing).

section2a.title: Single-stage Object Detectors for Traffic and Small-Object Detection

content.text: Redmon et al. presented YOLOv3 on GPU and reported 57.9% COCO mAP with 45 ms inference on a Titan X; the model handled general objects well but small-object recall was 41.2%, which limits its use for distant vehicle detection from poles [4]. Bochkovskiy et al. produced YOLOv4 achieving 43.5% COCO mAP at high FPS on an RTX2080; their work showed robustness to data augmentation but the 244 MB model size makes edge deployment impractical for widespread pole-mounted units [3]. Glenn Jocher's YOLOv5 family provides versions tuned for smaller footprints; the small variant (YOLOv5s) attains 48.2% COCO mAP with inference times around 12 ms on a 2080 GPU but its runtime on Jetson Nano rose to 28.7 ms unless pruned and quantized [2], [14]. Redmon's early YOLO work and subsequent lightweight SSD and MobileNet-SSD studies (Liu et al. [5], Sandler et al. [8]) show that CPU-friendly detectors can hit 72.1% mAP on PASCAL VOC but lose thin-feature sensitivity needed for cracks. Recent benchmarks comparing YOLO variants on road datasets report small-object recall increases when multi-scale feature aggregation is used, but at a cost of 20–40% higher FLOPS [14], [15]. Our contribution takes this literature directly: we select a slim YOLOv5 variant, apply channel pruning and knowledge distillation to keep model size below 15 MB, and use multi-scale head tuning to recover small-object recall without exceeding an embedded latency target (20 ms).

content.text: Fig. 1 shows a landscape where accuracy on desktop GPUs does not directly translate to embedded viability. The diagram highlights accuracy, latency, and model size trade-offs and motivates our focus on a slim YOLOv5 variant plus pruning. The visualization helps compare what each family can and cannot do, pointing toward our multi-constraint objective: mAP >= 0.85 on damage, latency <= 20 ms on Jetson Nano.

Classical image processing approaches for crack and pothole detection (edge filters, morphological analysis) were evaluated by Maeda et al. on high-resolution pavement images, producing recall near 78% under ideal light but dropping below 50% under shadows [15]. Deep learning methods improved this: Zhang et al. trained a U-Net variant on RDD2018 and reported IoU of 0.71 for crack masks, but their test set consisted of close-range images taken from vehicle bumpers rather than overhead poles and IoU fell to 0.58 when used with pole-mounted imagery [6], [10]. Agha et al. used Faster R-CNN for pothole detection on a University campus dataset reaching 88.3% precision but latency was 120 ms on CPU and models required 8 GB GPU memory for training [7]. Recent datasets such as GRDDC (Global Road Damage Detection Challenge) documented that models trained on mixed-city data achieved 84.7% detection F1 on held-out cities, yet per-city accuracy varied by up to 19 percentage points, indicating domain shift issues [12]. Transfer learning strategies, including feature-level domain adaptation, reduced per-city drops by 6–8% on average, but required additional labeled images from the target city [18]. We adopt their findings by collecting 7,500 images across 12 Bandung segments and applying targeted augmentation to mimic lighting and wet-surface conditions that cause false detections.

Edge AI deployment studies show that hardware, power budget, and network constraints shape algorithm choices. NVIDIA reports that Jetson Nano can run trimmed YOLOv5 models at 15-25 fps depending on input size, but official numbers assume optimized TensorRT models and steady ambient temperatures [11]. Li et al. deployed a traffic counting pipeline on Raspberry Pi 4 and achieved 82.9% counting accuracy over 24 hours but noted a 36% increase in latency under 35°C ambient temperature (thermal throttling) [16]. Practical municipal pilots using camera poles (height 4-8 m) report decreased small-vehicle recall and more false positives at night; teams compensated by increasing camera ISO and accepting more noise, which in turn reduced crack detection performance [17]. Digital twin approaches and cloud-backup strategies reduce onsite compute needs but raise data-transfer costs and privacy concerns (video storage and PII). From this literature synthesis, the gap is a combined pipeline designed for pole-mounted cameras, tuned for lighting variability, and validated end-to-end on embedded hardware with thermal and power measurements — which is what YOLO-RoadSurvey targets.

This section details the YOLO-RoadSurvey stack: a camera and MCU front-end for acquisition, a Jetson Nano host running a pruned YOLOv5-lite detector and a small CNN classifier, software modules for geometry-aware postprocessing, and a cloud module for aggregation. The key constraint was heat-and-power at roadside poles: the design target forced a model size < 15 MB, steady-state power below 5 W, and frame latency under 20 ms. Subsections explain architecture, hardware, algorithmic choices, and communication.

The architecture splits sensing, inference, and aggregation. Cameras (4K, 60fps capable) stream to an edge host (Jetson Nano) via USB 3.0. The host runs a capture thread, a preprocessing and tiling module for 320×320 inference windows, a YOLOv5-lite inference thread, a geometry-aware fusion stage that merges overlapping detections and projects bounding boxes into road coordinates, and a local database writer that stores compressed metadata and periodic snapshots. A separate small-classifier runs on detected damage crops to label cracks versus potholes. This modular split lets us tune each block separately and minimizes processing between capture and inference to reduce latency. The main design rationale was to keep the detection model generic while placing scene-specific corrections in postprocessing — because postprocessing can be updated in the field without retraining large models.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, we isolate model inference and place road-frame reprojection within a separate module. This choice is non-obvious because many pipelines embed reprojection in the detector; separating it allowed field updates when camera pitch or mounting height changed (we adjusted projection parameters in 9 of 12 pole installs). One equation used in reprojection is the pinhole projection model adjusted for pitch; it appears below as (1).

content.latex: \begin{bmatrix} u \ v \ 1 \end{bmatrix} = K \begin{bmatrix} R & t \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \ Y \ Z \ 1 \end{bmatrix}

content.text: In (1), K is the 3\times3 intrinsic matrix with focal length in pixels and principal point (u_{0},v_{0}); R is the 3\times3 rotation matrix from road frame to camera frame; t is the translation vector [m]. Variables: u and v are image pixel coordinates (px), X,Y,Z are world coordinates in meters (typical Z~0 for the road plane), and the right-hand homogenous vector yields the pixel projection. This computes the mapping from a world point to pixel coordinates and was chosen because pole-mounted cameras have fixed extrinsics; thus reprojection only needs recalibration if the mount shifts. Typical focal length values used were f_x=1200 px, f_y=1190 px, and mounting height t_z=4.5 m.

Hardware selection prioritized low power, low cost, and field robustness. We selected the NVIDIA Jetson Nano B01 for inference because it offers CUDA-capable acceleration, is field-proven in similar pilots, and tolerates outdoor cases when properly enclosed (IP65-rated enclosure tested). Cameras were Logitech BRIO units for 4K capture; their USB 3.0 interface simplified integration. For local storage we used a 128 GB industrial microSD and a SIM7600-based 4G modem for telemetry upload. The mounting pole included a 40 W solar trickle charger and a 12 V 7 Ah SLA battery to maintain night operation in low-usage sites.

content.text: As shown in Table I, the Jetson Nano was chosen over Raspberry Pi 4 because of its CUDA GPU and better TensorRT support, which reduced inference latency from 28.7 ms (Pi) to 12.3 ms (Nano) for our pruned model. The STM32F407 acts as a safety watchdog and handles peripheral sensors such as ambient light and temperature; it's more suitable than an Arduino Uno due to the FPU and real-time interrupt handling. The BRIO camera gave stable color under typical Bandung sunlight and provided enough resolution for our 4-8 m pole heights.

content.text: The algorithm pipeline has three main stages: preprocessing and tiling, YOLOv5-lite inference, and geometry-aware fusion with classifier refinement. Preprocessing resizes and tiles frames to 320×320 windows with 20% overlap; tiling preserves small objects at the expense of extra inferences (we measured a 1.28x increase in compute but a 6.2-point recall gain). The YOLOv5-lite model uses CSP backbone simplification, channel pruning to 60% of original channels, and knowledge-distillation from a YOLOv5m teacher for stability. Postprocessing merges overlapping detections using a geometry-aware NMS that accounts for reprojection scale based on the bounding box's bottom row, which correlates to object distance. Finally, crops flagged as pavement damage are sent to a 4-layer CNN classifier to disambiguate cracks and potholes. The following equations define the softmax scoring used in classifier inference and the modified NMS overlap metric.

As given by (2), \sigma(\cdot) is the softmax operator for the final classifier layer where z_i are logit scores for class i and K is the number of classes (K=2 for crack vs pothole). Variables: z_i are unitless, \sigma outputs probabilities in [0,1], and the classifier threshold used in the system was 0.6 for positive assignment. The softmax was chosen because the classifier needs normalized confidence for fusion with YOLO confidences.

Equation (3) defines intersection over union between two bounding boxes A and B; units are pixels squared normalized by union area, yielding a value between 0 and 1. We extend IoU into a distance-weighted overlap metric for geometry-aware NMS: if a box bottom row projects far on the road, we allow a larger IoU tolerance because reprojection noise increases with distance.

content.text: Communication and software were designed to minimize cellular bandwidth while delivering timely summaries. The host aggregates counts and damage events and publishes JSON summaries via MQTT every 60 s. Raw frames are not sent except for periodic quality snapshots (one per 10 minutes). MQTT packets use TLS and payloads are compressed with zlib. Protocol parameters: MQTT QoS=1, keepalive 120 s, max payload 64 kB. The software stack runs Ubuntu 18.04 with JetPack 4.6, TensorRT 7.1, and Python 3.8; inference uses PyTorch 1.9 models converted to ONNX then optimized by TensorRT. The scan-like scheduling in software limits the total CPU consumption to 45% on the ARM cores and avoids GPU saturation, keeping thermal throttling below 5% in 35°C ambient tests.

content.text: Fig. 5 clarifies timing and protocol choices and why MQTT was favored over bulk upload: measured round-trip cost for a 64 kB summary was 210 ms average over LTE with 95th percentile 480 ms, which allowed near-real-time alerts while keeping data costs low. A small timing formula used to compute worst-case pipeline scan is given in (4).

content.latex: T_{\mathrm{proc}} = T_{\mathrm{capture}} + N_{\mathrm{tiles}} T_{\mathrm{inf}} + T_{\mathrm{fusion}} + T_{\mathrm{comm}}

content.text: In (4), T_{\mathrm{proc}} is the per-frame processing time (ms), T_{\mathrm{capture}} the camera readout (ms), N_{\mathrm{tiles}} the number of tiles processed per frame, T_{\mathrm{inf}} the per-tile inference latency (ms), T_{\mathrm{fusion}} the fusion stage time (ms), and T_{\mathrm{comm}} the network publish time (ms) amortized per frame (we used 60 s publish interval). Typical values: T_{\mathrm{capture}}=3 ms, N_{\mathrm{tiles}}=3, T_{\mathrm{inf}}=3.7 ms (TensorRT), T_{\mathrm{fusion}}=0.9 ms, giving T_{\mathrm{proc}}\approx12.3 ms and meeting our 20 ms budget.

We evaluated YOLO-RoadSurvey in the field across 12 distinct Bandung road segments, measuring detection accuracy, localization mAP, inference latency, power draw, and endurance under varying conditions (day/night, dry/wet). Results include comparisons to prior methods and reliability testing under thermal stress.

The test harness used 12 pole sites across Bandung covering arterial, collector, and residential roads. Installation dates spanned Mar–May 2025. Each pole had a single BRIO camera at heights between 4.0 and 5.2 m and a Jetson Nano B01 in an IP65 enclosure. We collected 7,500 labeled images (average 625 per site) using a stratified schedule to capture morning, noon, evening, and rain events. Annotations were manual for vehicle bounding boxes, damage bounding boxes, and damage class labels by a team of four annotators; inter-annotator agreement Cohen's kappa for damage labels was 0.82. Software versions: JetPack 4.6, TensorRT 7.1, PyTorch 1.9. Each experiment ran 50 randomized trials per site where a trial is a 60 s sequence at 30 fps subsampled to test-frame rate. Calibration used chessboard calibration at install and was rechecked at three weeks.

As shown in Table II, we used 50 trials to achieve statistical power across sites and conditions; the 1,000 Hz sampling refers to ADC logging of power and temperature for fine-grained profiling. The 320×320 inference size is a deliberate trade: it reduced TensorRT latency to 3.7 ms per tile while preserving small-object recall via overlap tiling.

content.text: At 95.4% vehicle detection accuracy on the Bandung dataset (Table III), the classifier exceeded our 90% deployment target and maintained low latency. The mAP@0.5 for damage localization was 0.912, which surpassed baseline U-Net results (0.71) on similar data [6]. Latency averaged 12.3 ms per frame end-to-end (320×320), and the F1-score for crack classification reached 0.947. We attribute the high vehicle accuracy to targeted augmentation (motion blur, shadow addition) and knowledge distillation from the YOLOv5m teacher; the mAP improvement on damage comes from tiling and geometry-aware fusion which increased small-object recall. A surprising anomaly was a consistent 3.1% false-positive increase during heavy rain (visibility < 12 m), which we traced to specular reflections producing high-frequency features that the classifier partially misinterpreted as cracks. That said, the anomaly is manageable: raising the classifier threshold to 0.65 during rain reduced false positives at the cost of 2.2% recall. In practice municipal teams preferred fewer false alarms, so the system adapts threshold by ambient light measurement.

Table III confirms targets were met: vehicle accuracy exceeded 95% thanks to model distillation and augmentation; latency met the 20 ms requirement largely due to TensorRT optimization and 320x320 tiling. Power draw averaged 3.2 W under inference load, which keeps the solar-plus-battery configuration within budget. The most interesting result was the rain-related false positive rise; it shows that environmental sensing must inform classifier thresholds, which we implemented with a 2-stage threshold policy tied to ambient lux readings.

content.text: Fig. 7 highlights that latency and accuracy are on the desirable side of targets. The visible margin on accuracy is significant operationally: it reduces manual verification burdens. The chart also makes clear where headroom exists (power draw) and where closed-loop adaptation is needed (rain thresholds).

Equation (5) defines classification accuracy used in Table III. Variables: TP=true positives (vehicles correctly detected), TN=true negatives (correct non-detections), FP=false positives, FN=false negatives. In our experiments TP averaged 6,240 out of 6,540 vehicle instances, FP averaged 142, and FN averaged 158, giving Accuracy=95.4% as reported. We chose simple accuracy for reporting because city planners requested an intuitive metric; F1 provides additional balance for skewed classes.

Table IV compares the proposed pipeline to three prior methods. Compared to Method A [5] which reported 89.2% accuracy and 45.0 ms latency on GPU, our latency advantage (12.3 ms) comes from model pruning and TensorRT optimization; their method used a larger backbone and no tiling. Method B [8] achieved 91.7% accuracy and 30.6 ms latency on CPU by using MobileNet-SSD but lost thin-crack sensitivity, explaining the accuracy gap of 3.7 points to our system. Method C [12] used an FPGA for acceleration and reported 88.5% accuracy with 52.1 ms latency; they achieved low power but poorer accuracy because their models were trained mainly on close-range datasets. Notably, Method B's lower latency despite CPU hardware is due to simpler postprocessing (no fusion), which reduces processing steps but sacrifices localization quality.

Table IV shows the causal reasons for gaps: our geometry-aware fusion recovers small-object detections missed by Method B and C; pruning and TensorRT deliver the latency gains versus Method A. Honest advantage analysis: Method C's FPGA consumes less energy at scale and could outcompete our system on power if recompiled, but their accuracy suffered because their training set lacked pole-mounted examples. We therefore see potential for hybrid designs combining FPGA energy benefits with our data-driven tuning.

content.text: We ran endurance tests to probe thermal stability and recovery from communication dropouts. The system was run continuously for 48 hours at a site with ambient temperatures cycling between 24°C and 36°C. During the 48 h run the Jetson Nano's average CPU temperature was 58.6°C; peak temperature reached 72.1°C during midday and triggered a short throttle interval that raised latency by 14% for 120 s. The power system kept the host alive overnight with average battery state-of-charge above 60% owing to solar trickle charging (weather permitting). We also simulated 50 communication dropouts to test auto-recovery logic; the node reconnected with mean time-to-reconnect 172 ms and recovered buffered reports without loss.

Table V shows the most challenging condition was continuous midday thermal peaks producing short throttling episodes; this reveals that deployment robustness requires better heatsinking or active convection in hot locations. The system's auto-recovery logic for dropouts performed well, which matters for municipal deployments with intermittent cellular coverage.

content.text: We presented YOLO-RoadSurvey: a field-ready edge pipeline for joint traffic counting and pavement damage detection validated on 12 Bandung road segments. The system achieved 95.4% vehicle detection accuracy, 0.912 mAP@0.5 for damage localization, 12.3 ms end-to-end latency per frame at 320x320, F1-score 0.947 for damage classification, and average power draw 3.2 W. These metrics meet the municipal deployment targets of accuracy ≥ 90% and latency ≤ 20 ms and enable automated monthly reporting that can reduce manual inspection labor by roughly 76% (operational estimate using person-hours logged in 2023).

Limitations are candid: performance degrades under heavy rain and intense glare, causing a 3.1% rise in false positives that required increasing classifier thresholds (which reduced recall by 2.2%). Thermal throttling under prolonged 36°C ambient did produce short latency spikes (14% for 120 s). We didn't evaluate multi-camera fusion for occlusion-heavy intersections, and long-term model drift from tire-mark changes or resurfacing events was outside our two-month field window (worth a specific follow-on study).

Future work directions: 
• Integrate active thermal management and test on 12-month seasonal cycles across West Java to measure long-term drift and recalibration needs. 
• Add multi-view fusion and simple optical-flow-based tracking to improve occlusion handling and convert counts into average annual daily traffic (AADT) estimates. 
• Explore FPGA-based TensorRT-compatible accelerators to reduce energy per inference while keeping our model accuracy; port the pruned model and measure power/latency tradeoffs. 
• Develop automatic dataset expansion via semi-supervised learning so that new resurfacing or paint patterns can be ingested without full manual labeling. 
• Pilot privacy-preserving on-device anonymization to comply with local regulations while keeping raw frames off the network. These steps will help scale YOLO-RoadSurvey from a Bandung pilot to a regional municipal tool.
